Munajat-e-Maqbool

Monday

Third manzil · supplications 86 to 116

Opening praise

In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

We praise You, O best of those in whom hope is placed and most generous of those from whom anything is sought, for teaching us Munajat-e-Maqbool, which brings nearness to Allah, and the supplications of the Messenger. Send perfect blessings upon him for as long as the west and east winds blow, and branches spring from their roots. Then we ask You for what we are about to recite. Ours is to ask, and Yours is to grant acceptance.

How to read

Read this opening invocation before each daily portion. Begin on Saturday, read one portion each day in order, and complete the cycle on Friday.

Swipe right to left to turn the page

In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

Supplication86

Patience, gratitude and humility

O Allah, make me patient and make me grateful. Make me small in my own eyes and great in the eyes of others.

Original commentary 86

This Prophetic supplication teaches us to ask: O Allah, make me small in my own eyes and great in the eyes of others. It teaches that one should never consider oneself great, while also not debasing oneself before others. For the one who recites it, there is the glad tiding that he will not be disgraced before people in this world.

Sources and notesMonday · Prayer p. 59 · variant

Musnad al-Bazzar 4439

Variant. Al-Albani: daif, Daif al-Jami 1167. All four requests present; gratitude precedes patience in this route.

Ilal Ibn Abi Hatim 1978

Variant. Abu Hatim al-Razi: munkar, not known; Uqba is weak in hadith. Exact sequence appears, with Allahumma repeated.

The supplication is traceable to reports criticised as weak or munkar. The original commentary’s particular guarantee against worldly disgrace has not been verified in the cited sources.

Supplication87

Blessings and contentment

O Allah, place in our land its blessing, its beauty and its tranquillity. Do not deprive me of the blessing of what You have given me, and do not put me to trial through what You have withheld from me.

Sources and notesMonday · Prayer p. 59 · composite

Al-Tabarani, al-Mujam al-Awsat 4692

Component: Opening request for blessing, beauty and habitation in the land. Al-Haythami: its chain is good, Majma al-Zawaid 10/185. The entire opening clause matches this report.

Al-Tabarani, al-Mujam al-Awsat 7110

Component: Do not deprive me of the blessing of what You give, or try me through what You withhold. Al-Shawkani: narrators are those of the Sahih except Salama ibn Abi Hakima, whom he calls trustworthy (Tuhfat al-Dhakirin 458). Al-Tabarani’s text has haramtani; the quotation in the critical source has ahramtani, as in this compilation.

Two reports are joined. The assessment for the latter concerns its narrators and is not an explicit authentication of the whole report.

Supplication88

Beautiful character and a peaceful heart

O Allah, You have made my appearance beautiful, so make my character beautiful too. Remove the anger from my heart and protect me from trials that lead astray, for as long as You keep us alive.

Original commentary 88

This Prophetic supplication is to be recited when looking in a mirror. Its meaning is: O Allah, You have made my appearance beautiful; make my character beautiful too.

Sources and notesMonday · Prayer p. 60 · composite

Musnad Ahmad 3823

Component: Opening request for beautiful character. Al-Haythami: narrators of the Sahih except Awsaja ibn al-Rammah, who is trustworthy (Majma al-Zawaid 10/176). Exact opening appears in Ahmad.

Musnad Ahmad 26576

Component: Remove anger and protect from misleading trials throughout life. Ahmad Shakir: sahih chain, Umdat al-Tafsir 1/355. The closing two clauses including ma ahyaytana match the supplication taught to Umm Salama.

Al-Bayhaqi, al-Daawat al-Kabir 489

Parallel only: Mirror occasion stated in the original commentary, not the whole compiled dua. Al-Bayhaqi: weak chain (al-Daawat al-Kabir 2/82–83). The mirror-specific report is weak. Ahmad 24392 transmits the character prayer without specifying that occasion.

Two separate supplications are combined; the ending’s plural pronoun is present in the reported wording. The request for beautiful character is transmitted independently, while al-Bayhaqi grades the report specifying a mirror as weak. The stronger general report does not establish that particular occasion.

This short supplication should be kept on one's tongue at all times. Its meaning is: O Allah, grant me faith and the declaration of faith at the time of death.

Al-Tabarani, al-Mujam al-Awsat 1886

Excerpt. Al-Haythami: Ibn Lahia is in the chain, his hadith is hasan, and the other narrators are trustworthy (Majma al-Zawaid 10/185). The closing prayer includes the words inda al-mamat, meaning at death.

The quoted narrator assessment is distinguished from an explicit judgement that the entire report is sahih.

Supplication92

Pardon and protection on every side

O Allah, I ask You for pardon and well-being in my religion, my worldly life, my family and my wealth. O Allah, cover my faults and replace my fear with security. O Allah, protect me from before me, from behind me, from my right, from my left and from above me. I seek refuge in Your greatness from being overtaken from beneath me.

Original commentary 92

When his uncle Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) asked repeatedly, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) urged him to recite this supplication. It is a concise and mighty prayer; whoever has it accepted will enjoy ease in both worlds. Its meaning is: O Allah, I ask You for forgiveness and well-being in religion and worldly life.

Sources and notesMonday · Prayer p. 61 · excerpt

Sunan Abi Dawud 5074

Variant. Sahih (al-Albani), as displayed by Sunnah.com. Singular/plural wording variants are recorded in the hadith itself.

Jami al-Tirmidhi 3514

Parallel only: The original commentary’s story of al-Abbas asking for a supplication. Al-Tirmidhi: sahih; Sahih (Darussalam) displayed by Sunnah.com. This story teaches asking for well-being in this life and the Hereafter; it does not transmit all the words of dua 92.

The collection omits the initial request for well-being in this world and the Hereafter and uses singular forms for faults and fears. Regarding the original commentary: The al-Abbas report recommends asking Allah for well-being in this world and the Hereafter. The fuller wording printed here is separately narrated from Ibn Umar.

Supplication93

Mercy and putting affairs right

O Ever-Living, O Sustainer of all, by Your mercy I seek help. Set right for me all my affairs, and do not leave me to myself even for the blink of an eye.

Original commentary 93

This supplication has the distinction that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) frequently recited it. Our teachers and spiritual elders have described frequent recitation of this prayer as a remedy for removing every hardship and anxiety.

Sources and notesMonday · Prayer p. 62 · exact

Al-Nasai, al-Sunan al-Kubra 10330

Exact. Siddiq Hasan Khan: chain hasan sahih, Husn al-Uswa 512; al-Hakim 2000 also authenticates it. The full supplication matches al-Nasai’s text.

Al-Nasai’s report is also numbered 10405 in another edition. The original commentary’s statement about removing every hardship is devotional counsel attributed to teachers and elders, not a separately verified guarantee attached to reciting these words.

Sources and notesMonday · Prayer p. 62 · variant

Al-Tabarani, al-Mujam al-Kabir 8027

Variant: all apart from shortened time clause and word variant. Al-Albani: very weak, al-Silsila al-Daifa 6253. The same closing passage is in a longer morning/evening prayer, with taqbalani and a morning/evening qualification.

Variant: The taqilani variant and closing passage. Al-Haythami: Faddal ibn Jubayr is weak, with agreement on his weakness (Majma al-Zawaid 10/120). Al-Shajari’s version has taqilani. This compilation omits the report’s morning/evening qualification.

The supporting report is weak/very weak according to the named assessments; this is not authenticated by its familiar phrases.

Reflect on this supplication's meaning: it asks for every good of the morning, midday and evening. At the end, it gathers everything into this request: O Most Merciful of those who show mercy, grant us every good of this world and the Hereafter.

A wording assembled from closely related weak versions. Ya Arham al-rahimin is recorded in the parallel version, not in Abd ibn Humayd 531.

O Allah, forgive my sin, make my home spacious for me, and bless my provision.

Original commentary 100

This prayer teaches us a wonderful request: forgive my sins, make my home spacious and comfortable, and bestow blessing and goodness in my provision. In these times of trials, keep the prayer's meaning firmly in mind. It teaches us that, to protect ourselves from trials, we should not go outside the four walls of our homes without need.

Exact. Al-Albani: weak. This assessment concerns the same Abu Musa wording and route. Parallel transmissions appear in Abu Yala 7273 and Ibn Abi Shayba 29391.

Supplication103

Light within and around us

O Allah, place light in my heart, light in my sight, light in my hearing, light to my right, light to my left, light behind me, and before me light.

Grant me light, and place light in my sinews, light in my flesh, light in my blood, light in my hair, light in my skin and light in my tongue. Place light within me, make my light great, and make me light. Place light above me and light below me. O Allah, grant me light.

Original commentary 103

The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) used to recite this Prophetic supplication in the morning. These are such beautiful words, asking: O Allah, place light in the heart, light in the eyes, light in the ears, and light to the right, to the left, above, below, in the flesh and in the blood. Light is sought in everything. This prayer for light has also been included among the Quranic supplications.

Sources and notesMonday · Prayer p. 66 · composite

Sahih al-Bukhari 6316

Component: Heart, sight, hearing, surrounding directions, grant me light; sinews, flesh, blood, hair and skin. Reported in Sahih al-Bukhari. The five body terms occur in Kurayb’s continuation after consulting a descendant of al-Abbas. The compilation rearranges clauses and uses shimali in place of yasari for the left side.

Sahih Muslim 763j

Component: Tongue, self, and make my light great; surrounding directions. Reported in Sahih Muslim. Twelve requests explicitly include fi lisani, fi nafsi, and azim li nuran.

Sahih Muslim 763h

Component: Make me light. Reported in Sahih Muslim. This version gives make me light without the narrator’s uncertainty found in another version.

Sahih Muslim 763l

Component: O Allah, grant me light; light above and below. Reported in Sahih Muslim. Closing atini nuran is explicit in the variant said when going out for prayer.

The compilation combines attested variants and changes their order. The wording is supported across Bukhari and Muslim, though it does not all occur in one version. This is a hadith prayer, not a Quran verse; the reference to Quranic supplications belongs to the original commentary.

Supplication104

Doors of mercy and provision

O Allah, open for us the doors of Your mercy, and make the doors of Your provision easy for us to enter.

Original commentary 104

By asking that the doors of mercy be opened and access to provision be made easy, this prayer teaches us that seeking this world and its attainment from Allah is a source of reward. This is also the supplication recited when entering the mosque. Alongside this, we ask that all doors of provision be made easy for us.

Sources and notesMonday · Prayer p. 68 · exact

Abu Awana, al-Mustakhraj 1236, quoted in al-Albani, Sahih Abi Dawud al-Umm 2/363

Locator: 1236; quotation 2/363. Exact. Al-Albani, Sahih Abi Dawud al-Umm 2/363: narrators trustworthy, but this wording and chain are shadh (anomalous). Al-Albani quotes Abu Awana’s report with its chain and both clauses in his critical discussion.

Sahih Muslim 713a

Component: Open for me the doors of Your mercy. Reported in Sahih Muslim. The mosque-entry formula uses singular li, meaning for me. It does not include the provision-doors clause; on leaving the mosque, Muslim transmits the request for Allah’s bounty.

Both clauses are traceable to an Abu Awana report, but al-Albani criticises that wording and chain as shadh, or anomalous. Sahih Muslim transmits the request for the doors of mercy on entering the mosque, without the provision clause. The original commentary’s mosque-entry attribution therefore requires this distinction.

Supplication109

O Allah, I am Your servant, the son of Your servant and the son of Your female servant. My forelock is in Your hand. Your command over me is carried out, and Your judgement concerning me is just. This is a lengthy prayer in which a person appeals through his servitude to Allah: O Allah, make the magnificent Qur'an the springtime of our hearts, the light of our eyes, and a means of removing our sorrow and worry.

Variant: all, including nur basari. Al-Albani: sahih, al-Silsila al-Sahiha 199; the same chain was called weak by Shuayb al-Arnaut in Takhrij al-Musnad 4318. Supplication112

Humble pleading and the prayer of Taif

O Allah, You hear my words, see where I am, and know what I conceal and what I reveal. Nothing of my affairs is hidden from You. I am afflicted and needy, crying for help and seeking refuge, fearful and apprehensive, acknowledging and confessing my sin.

I ask You as a destitute person asks, and I implore You as a humbled sinner implores. I call upon You as one who is fearful and afflicted, and as one whose neck is bowed before You, whose tears flow for You, whose body is humbled before You, and whose nose is lowered in submission to You. O Allah, do not leave me disappointed in calling upon You. Be compassionate and merciful to me, O best of those who are asked, and O best of those who give!

Original commentary 112

This lengthy prayer has a profound meaning. In it, a person presents himself before Allah in this way: O Allah, nothing about me is hidden from You. I am afflicted, needy, crying for help and seeking refuge. I am fearful and apprehensive; I acknowledge and confess my sins. I bring before You a plea of utter helplessness and a tearful prayer. O Allah, do not leave me unsuccessful or disappointed in these supplications.

O Allah, to You I complain of my weakness, my lack of means, and my low standing in people's eyes. O Most Merciful of those who show mercy, to whom do You entrust me? To an enemy who attacks me, or to someone close to me whom You have given control over my affairs? If You are not displeased with me, I do not mind; yet the well-being You grant is more ample for me.

Original source note 113 · on supplication 112

This transmitted prayer was made at Ta'if, at the most painful and distressing time in the Prophet's life, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Amid all those difficulties, he asked: O Allah, if You are pleased with me through these hardships and troubles, I do not mind them. O Allah, my request is that You grant me peace and tranquillity.

Sources and notesMonday · Prayer p. 72 · composite

Al-Tabarani, al-Mujam al-Kabir 11405

Component: Opening through O best of those asked and best of givers. Al-Albani: daif, Daif al-Jami 1186. The opening supplication is a close variant of the reported Farewell Pilgrimage prayer.

Al-Tabari, Tarikh al-Rusul wa-l-Muluk 1/554

Component: From To You I complain of my weakness through Your well-being is more expansive for me. Shuayb al-Arnaut: mursal; the prayer itself is excepted from his favourable narrator comment on the surrounding account. Ibn Ishaq’s Taif narrative supplies the far-away person/enemy and Lord of the weak wording, with source saying walakin instead of ghayra anna.

Al-Tabarani, al-Mujam al-Kabir 14764

Parallel only: Taif complaint and plea for well-being. Al-Albani: daif, Daif al-Jami 1182. Related connected report has different wording, including enemy/relative.

Two prayers are joined. The Taif association concerns the portion beginning O Allah, to You I complain of my weakness. Its transmission is not established as sahih by the cited assessments, and the combined entry is not one authenticated narration.

Component: Faith reaching the heart; what Allah has written; contentment with one’s allotted life. Al-Haythami: Abu Mahdi Said ibn Sinan is weak, Majma al-Zawaid 10/184. Core prayer recorded; the additional yaqinan sadiqan is not in this text.

Ilal Ibn Abi Hatim 2061

Component: Faith in the heart and truthful certainty, with contentment. Abu Hatim al-Razi: munkar. The additional truthful certainty wording appears in the reported Adam supplication; the narrative’s rewards are not authenticated.

Closely related formulations from critically weak reports are combined. The promised outcomes in the surrounding Adam narrative are not established by a sound transmission.

Supplication115

Praise beyond our words

O Allah, all praise belongs to You, as You Yourself say, and better than anything we say.

Sources and notesMonday · Prayer p. 75 · excerpt

Jami al-Tirmidhi 3520

Excerpt. Al-Tirmidhi: its chain is not strong; Darussalam: daif. Exact selected passage appears within the Arafah supplication.

Both 115 and 117 are excerpts of this same report; the shared source has a weak chain according to the cited assessments.

Supplication116

Protection from moral evils and trials

O Allah, I seek refuge in You from blameworthy character, deeds, desires and illnesses. We seek refuge in You from every evil from which Your Prophet Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sought refuge; from a bad neighbour in a permanent dwelling, for a neighbour in the desert moves away; from an enemy's domination and the gloating of enemies; from hunger, for it is a wretched bedfellow; and from treachery, for it is a wretched inner companion;

from turning back on our heels or being drawn away from our religion; from trials, both those that are apparent and those that are hidden; from a bad day, a bad night, a bad hour and a bad companion.

Original commentary 116

This transmitted supplication teaches an important lesson by seeking protection from blameworthy character, deeds and harmful illnesses. It also teaches us to seek protection from an enemy's domination and from all trials, whether outward or inward. This prayer asks for sound conduct and character. It also teaches us to seek refuge from every evil from which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sought refuge. We are also taught to ask: O Allah, protect us from outward and inward trials, and keep us safe from a bad day, a bad night, a bad hour and a bad companion. Read this supplication with its meaning and examine your own condition: see how the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, taught us this beautiful prayer, encompassing our needs and necessities.

Sources and notesMonday · Prayer p. 76 · composite

Jami al-Tirmidhi 3591

Component: Opening: blameworthy character, deeds and desires. Sahih (Darussalam); al-Tirmidhi: hasan gharib. The Arabic has character, deeds and desires, but not illnesses.

Al-Tabarani al-Mujam al-Kabir 36

Component: Opening: illnesses as well as character, deeds and desires. Ibn Hajar: hasan in Hidayat al-Ruwat 3/23. Original al-Tabarani 19/19, no.36 reads jannibni and includes all four categories; the compilation uses audhu bika.

Jami al-Tirmidhi 3521

Component: Refuge from what the Prophet Muhammad sought refuge from. Daif (Darussalam); al-Tirmidhi: hasan gharib. Close wording; the report has istaadha bika minhu, with bika omitted in the compilation.

Sunan an-Nasai 5502

Component: Bad neighbour in a permanent residence; desert neighbour moves away. Hasan (Darussalam). Report instructs the hearers to seek refuge, uses dar al-maqam and ends yatahawwalu anka; this compilation turns it into first-person prayer, uses al-muqama and omits anka.

Sunan an-Nasai 5475

Component: Enemy domination and enemies gloating. Hasan (Darussalam). Exact two clauses excerpted from a prayer also mentioning overwhelming debt.

Sunan Abi Dawud 1547

Component: Hunger as a bad bedfellow and betrayal as a bad inner companion. Hasan (al-Albani). Compilation abbreviates the repeated refuge formula and fa-innaha.

Sahih al-Bukhari 6593

Component: Turning back on our heels or being tried away from our religion. Reported in Sahih al-Bukhari as the words of Ibn Abi Mulayka. This sentence is explicitly the supplication of the sub-narrator Ibn Abi Mulayka after the Prophetic report, not itself Prophetic speech.

Sahih Muslim 2867

Component: Trials, apparent and hidden. Reported in Sahih Muslim. Exact phrase in the Prophetic instruction and the Companions response.

Al-Tabarani al-Mujam al-Kabir 810

Component: Bad day, night, hour and companion. Al-Haythami, Majma al-Zawaid 7/223: its narrators are trustworthy. The original text at 17/294 contains these four clauses, followed by a bad-neighbour clause.

This compilation joins several reports with differing grades and small grammatical adaptations. The request against turning back and being tried in religion is Ibn Abi Mulayka’s own prayer, quoted after a Prophetic report in Bukhari. The complete sequence is not one continuous Prophetic supplication, despite the impression given by the original commentary.

ClosingDurood

O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad, the unlettered Prophet, and upon his family, and grant them peace in abundance.

Note from the Urdu edition

The Urdu edition narrates from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said: Whoever recites this blessing eighty times on Friday after the Asr prayer, before rising from his place, will have eighty years of sins forgiven, and the reward of eighty years of worship will be recorded for him.

Reference review

The specific promise quoted above has not been established as sound in this review. Al-Sakhawi records the post-ʿAsr wording and discusses weak chains and a disputed related grading. It should not be presented as a guaranteed eighty-year reward. See general reference G3.

General blessings upon the Prophet are supported by Qur’an 33:56. A general encouragement does not by itself establish a particular count, occasion or reward.
